title: Problem Overview
content: **Erdős Problem #903** asks: for n = p² + p + 1 with p a prime power, if a block design has t > n blocks, must t ≥ n + p? The answer is YES, proved by Erdős-Fowler-Sós-Wilson (1985). The problem reveals a rigidity phenomenon: once a block design exceeds the projective-plane minimum, its block count must jump by at least p.
mathContext: Block designs with the pair-coverage property (every pair in exactly one block) are also called *pairwise balanced designs* (PBDs). The parameter n = p² + p + 1 is the point count of a projective plane of order p, and the de Bruijn-Erdős theorem (1948) establishes t ≥ n as a universal lower bound. This problem asks whether the lower bound is essentially the only achievable value near n — answering yes, with a gap of width p.

crossReferences.description: Erdős #734 studies PBDs with bounded block frequencies — a direct generalization of the pair-coverage property formalized here
Erdős #722 formalizes Steiner systems S(r,k,n), which are the uniform specialization of the block designs studied here

title: BlockDesign Structure
content: A block design on {1,...,n} is a collection of subsets (blocks) such that every pair of distinct elements is contained in exactly one block. This is the 2-(n, k, 1) design property when blocks are uniform, or a pairwise balanced design (PBD) in the non-uniform case.
mathContext: The structure `BlockDesign n` captures a PBD(n) — a partition of the complete graph K_n into cliques (blocks). The `pair_coverage` axiom encodes λ = 1 pair-coverage: for every distinct x, y ∈ {1,...,n}, there exists a unique block containing both. This is equivalent to saying the blocks form the lines of a *linear space* on n points. The formalization uses `Finset (Finset ℕ)` for blocks, restricting to finite set-system combinatorics.

crossReferences.description: Erdős #734 also formalizes PBD structure and uses the de Bruijn-Erdős lower bound m ≥ n
Erdős #732 studies which block-size sequences are compatible with valid PBD structure

title: numBlocks
content: The number of blocks t = |blocks| in a design, computed as `D.blocks.card`. This is the central parameter: the problem asks which values of t are achievable.
mathContext: In design theory notation, t corresponds to the parameter b (number of blocks). The de Bruijn-Erdős theorem gives b ≥ v (number of points), and this problem asks about the gap structure of achievable b-values when v = p² + p + 1.

title: IsPrimePower
content: A natural number q is a prime power if q = p^k for some prime p and k ≥ 1. Prime powers are exactly the orders for which projective planes are known to exist (via finite field constructions).
mathContext: The prime power conjecture states that projective planes exist if and only if the order is a prime power. The 'if' direction is classical (Galois, 1830s): PG(2, GF(q)) gives a projective plane of order q for every prime power q. The 'only if' direction is wide open — the Bruck-Ryser theorem (1949) eliminates some orders (e.g., 6), and computer search eliminated order 10 (Lam, 1991), but no general non-existence proof is known for non-prime-power orders.

title: IsProjectivePlaneSize
content: n has projective plane size if n = q² + q + 1 for some prime power q. The sequence begins 7, 13, 21, 31, 57, 73, 91, 111, 133, ... corresponding to q = 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, ...
mathContext: The formula n = q² + q + 1 counts both the points and lines of PG(2, GF(q)). It arises because a projective plane of order q has q + 1 points on each line, q + 1 lines through each point, and q² + q + 1 points total (equivalently, the number of 1-dimensional subspaces of GF(q)³). Note q = 6 and q = 10 are excluded since no projective planes of those orders exist.

title: de Bruijn-Erdős Theorem
content: Every block design on n ≥ 2 points has at least n blocks. This foundational 1948 result of de Bruijn and Erdős provides the universal lower bound t ≥ n for pairwise balanced designs.
mathContext: The original proof by de Bruijn and Erdős (1948) uses a clever double-counting argument. For each point x, let r_x be the number of blocks containing x. Then Σ r_x = Σ |A_i| (counting incidences), and Σ r_x(r_x - 1) = n - 1 for each x (each pair through x is in exactly one block). By Cauchy-Schwarz on the r_x, one obtains t ≥ n. Equality holds iff all r_x are equal — which characterizes projective planes and near-pencil designs.

crossReferences.description: Erdős #734 also axiomatizes the de Bruijn-Erdős bound as the foundation for PBD block-count analysis

title: IsMinimalDesign
content: A design is minimal if it achieves exactly t = n blocks — the de Bruijn-Erdős lower bound is tight. For n = q² + q + 1, projective planes are the primary examples.
mathContext: The de Bruijn-Erdős equality case analysis shows that minimal designs on n ≥ 2 points are either (a) *near-pencils*: one block of size n-1 and n-1 blocks of size 2, or (b) *symmetric designs*: all blocks have the same size k = √(n - 1) + 1, and n must satisfy n - 1 = k(k-1). Case (b) gives projective planes when n = q² + q + 1.

title: Minimal Design Uniformity
content: In a minimal design (t = n) that is not a near-pencil, all blocks have the same size k. This is a consequence of the de Bruijn-Erdős equality case.
mathContext: The uniformity of minimal designs connects to the theory of *symmetric 2-designs* (also called *symmetric BIBDs*). A symmetric 2-(v, k, λ) design has exactly v blocks, each of size k, with every pair in λ blocks. The case λ = 1 gives projective planes: a symmetric 2-(q²+q+1, q+1, 1) design. The Fisher inequality gives b ≥ v for any 2-design, and equality b = v forces a strong regularity structure.

title: ProjectivePlane Structure
content: A projective plane of order q has q² + q + 1 points and q² + q + 1 lines, with each line containing q + 1 points and every two points determining a unique line. The Fano plane (q = 2) is the smallest example.
mathContext: The axioms capture the incidence structure PG(2, GF(q)): (1) `num_points` = q²+q+1 points, (2) `num_lines` = q²+q+1 lines (duality), (3) `line_size` = q+1 points per line, (4) `two_points_one_line` = the unique-line axiom. Missing from the formalization is the dual axiom (two lines meet in a unique point) — but this follows from the other axioms for finite planes. The formalization also omits *non-Desarguesian planes*, which exist for non-prime orders (the smallest is the Hall plane of order 9).

crossReferences.description: Erdős #664 constructs blocking sets inside PG(2,q), directly using the projective plane structure
Erdős #901 uses the Fano plane (PG(2,2)) as the extremal example for m(3) = 7

title: Projective Plane as Block Design
content: A projective plane of order q naturally gives a block design on n = q² + q + 1 points, where lines become blocks. This achieves the minimum t = n, showing the de Bruijn-Erdős bound is tight.
mathContext: The projective plane PG(2, GF(q)) yields a 2-(q²+q+1, q+1, 1) design — a *Steiner 2-design*. Its lines partition the pairs of points, each line containing q+1 points and covering C(q+1, 2) = q(q+1)/2 pairs. The total pairs C(q²+q+1, 2) = (q²+q+1)(q²+q)/2 are covered by (q²+q+1) lines, each covering q(q+1)/2 pairs, confirming exact coverage.

crossReferences.description: Projective planes are Steiner systems S(2, q+1, q²+q+1), a special case of the S(r,k,n) studied in Erdős #722

title: EFSW 1985: The Gap Theorem
content: Erdős-Fowler-Sós-Wilson (1985) proved the central conjecture: for a block design on n = p² + p + 1 points, if t > n then t ≥ n + p. This creates a forbidden interval (n, n + p) of unachievable block counts.
mathContext: The proof by Erdős, Fowler, Sós, and Wilson uses a detailed analysis of the *replication numbers* r_x (blocks through point x) and *intersection numbers* (|A_i ∩ A_j|). When t > n, the replication numbers must deviate from the uniform value q + 1 (the projective-plane value). The deviation is quantified using the variance Σ(r_x - r̄)², and a careful algebraic argument shows that sufficient deviation forces t ≥ n + p. The paper appeared in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, 1985.

title: EFSW Strong Bound
content: Unless the design comes from a 'broken' projective plane, the gap is even larger: t ≥ n + ⌈1.148p⌉. Breaking a line means replacing one (q+1)-point line with q+1 singleton blocks, increasing the block count by q.
mathContext: A *broken projective plane* of order q takes PG(2, GF(q)), removes one line L (containing q+1 points), and replaces it with q+1 singleton blocks {x} for each x ∈ L. The resulting design has (q²+q+1) - 1 + (q+1) = q²+2q+1 = (q+1)² blocks. Since (q+1)² = (q²+q+1) + q, this achieves exactly t = n + p (where p = q is the order). The constant c ≈ 1.148 means that all other non-minimal designs have an even wider gap, forcing t ≥ n + ⌈1.148p⌉.

title: achievableBlocks
content: The set of values t that can be achieved by some block design on p² + p + 1 points: achievableBlocks(p) = { t | ∃ D : BlockDesign(p²+p+1), D.numBlocks = t }.
mathContext: Characterizing achievableBlocks(p) is an open problem in design theory. Known elements include: n (via projective planes), n + p (via broken projective planes), and larger values constructible by further 'breaking' or extending designs. The gap theorem says (n, n+p) ∩ achievableBlocks(p) = ∅. For q = 2 (n = 7), the achievable values are known to be {7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 21} (all designs on 7 points have been classified).

title: The Gap: Forbidden Block Counts
content: Values in the open interval (n, n+p) are NOT achievable by any block design on n = p² + p + 1 points. This is the core 'gap phenomenon' — the de Bruijn-Erdős bound is not merely tight but isolated.
mathContext: The gap phenomenon is analogous to spectral gaps in other areas of combinatorics. Compare with the Ramsey multiplicity problem (erdos-905): just as edge-triangle counts have gaps near the Turán threshold, block-design counts have gaps near the projective-plane minimum. Both reflect *rigidity* of extremal configurations — small perturbations from the extremal structure force large parameter jumps.

crossReferences.description: Erdős #905 studies a similar gap phenomenon for edge-triangle multiplicities above the Turán threshold

title: first_above_n (Proved)
content: The first achievable value above n is at least n + p. This is a direct consequence of `gap_theorem`: any t ∈ achievableBlocks(p) with t > n must satisfy t ≥ n + p, since all intermediate values are forbidden.
mathContext: The proof is a clean application of proof by contradiction: assume t > n and t < n + p, then gap_theorem gives t ∉ achievableBlocks(p), contradicting the hypothesis. This is one of the few fully-proved results in the file (no sorry). The Lean proof uses `by_contra` and `push_neg` to convert the negation into the form needed by gap_theorem, then applies `exact` to close the goal.

title: Concrete Gap Examples
content: For p=2: n=7, gap is (7,9). For p=3: n=13, gap is (13,16). For p=4: n=21, gap is (21,25). For p=5: n=31, gap is (31,36). Each computed by `norm_num`.
mathContext: These examples illustrate the gap width growing linearly with p. For the Fano plane (p=2, n=7), the gap excludes only t=8, and indeed no PBD on 7 points has exactly 8 blocks. The first achievable value above 7 is 9 (a broken Fano plane: remove one line of 3 points and replace with 3 singletons, giving 7 - 1 + 3 = 9 blocks). For p=3 (PG(2,3), n=13), t=14 and t=15 are forbidden, and the broken plane gives t=16.

title: Is2Design
content: A 2-(v, k, 1) design is a block design where every block has exactly k elements. Also called a *balanced incomplete block design* (BIBD) or *Steiner 2-design* when λ = 1.
mathContext: The 2-design property adds uniformity to the PBD: all blocks have the same size k. This forces strong parameter relationships: bk(k-1) = v(v-1) (pair counting), and r(k-1) = v-1 (replication). When b = v (symmetric design), k = r and we get a projective plane. Fisher's inequality b ≥ v is the uniform analogue of de Bruijn-Erdős. The Is2Design predicate connects the general block design framework to the more structured theory of BIBDs.

crossReferences.description: Steiner systems S(2,k,v) are exactly the 2-(v,k,1) designs formalized here

title: Fisher's Inequality
content: For 2-designs with k ≥ 2, the number of blocks b ≥ v (number of points). This is the uniform specialization of the de Bruijn-Erdős theorem.
mathContext: Fisher's inequality (1940) was proved before de Bruijn-Erdős (1948) but applies only to uniform designs. The proof uses linear algebra: the *incidence matrix* N (v × b) satisfies NN^T = (r - λ)I + λJ, where r is the replication number and λ the pair coverage. Since r - λ > 0 (from k ≥ 2), NN^T has rank v, forcing b ≥ v. de Bruijn and Erdős extended this to non-uniform designs using a combinatorial (not linear-algebraic) argument.

title: de_bruijn_erdos_from_fisher (Proved)
content: For uniform block designs (2-designs), de Bruijn-Erdős follows directly from Fisher's inequality. The proof is a single application of `fisher_inequality`.
mathContext: This theorem demonstrates the logical relationship: Fisher's inequality ⊂ de Bruijn-Erdős. The converse fails — de Bruijn-Erdős applies to non-uniform designs where Fisher's linear-algebraic proof breaks down. The proof `exact fisher_inequality D k hk h` is a direct forwarding, showing that for the uniform case, Fisher's result is strictly stronger (as it provides additional structural information about the equality case).

title: erdos_903_summary (Proved)
content: The main summary theorem combining three results: (1) de Bruijn-Erdős: t ≥ n for all block designs, (2) projective plane achieves t = n, (3) EFSW: t > n implies t ≥ n + p. All three conjuncts are proved from the axioms.
mathContext: The proof structure uses `refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩` to split the conjunction into three goals. The first goal requires showing n ≥ 2 (needed by `de_bruijn_erdos`), which is proved from the prime power hypothesis: if q = p^k with p prime and k ≥ 1, then q ≥ 2, so q²+q+1 ≥ 7 ≥ 2. This is the most substantial sub-proof, using `calc` and `omega` tactics. The second goal is discharged by `projective_plane_design`, and the third by `efsw_1985`. This theorem serves as a certificate that the formalization captures the complete answer to Erdős Problem #903.
